title: Wilson Disease: Copper Tests and Why Ceruloplasmin Is Not Enough
summary: Explain how ATP7B failure traps copper, interpret ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, hepatic copper and Kayser-Fleischer rings together, and know why a normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude Wilson disease.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 27 Hit 2 and Trap 2 (first lesson for Ch. 27). Checked against Alkhouri 2023 (summary of the AASLD Wilson disease practice guidance) and Schroeder 2021. Nuances: ceruloplasmin in Wilson disease is typically < 14 mg/dL (normal > 20); KF rings are absent in ~60% of hepatic presentations. Not taught: the reviewer’s reason for normal ceruloplasmin (acute-phase rise with infection, pregnancy, oral contraceptives — Hit 12) and “serum copper is a poor screening test”, Menkes syndrome (Hit 3) — not in the sources read.

objectives: Explain how ATP7B failure leads to copper accumulation.
Interpret ceruloplasmin, 24-h urinary copper, hepatic copper and KF rings in combination.
Explain why a normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude Wilson disease.

scenes.title: A young liver, a normal ceruloplasmin
scenes.altText: An invented case: a 19-year-old with unexplained raised liver enzymes and a hand tremor. Serum ceruloplasmin 22 mg/dL (reference > 20). A colleague says “ceruloplasmin is normal, so it isn’t Wilson disease.” Question token: “Does a normal ceruloplasmin exclude Wilson disease — and which tests decide?”

cues.text: A 19-year-old has unexplained raised liver enzymes and a new hand tremor.
Serum ceruloplasmin comes back at 22, inside the reference range. A colleague says that rules out Wilson disease.
Does it? And which tests actually decide?

scenes.title: Where copper normally goes
scenes.altText: Copper pathway card (AASLD 2023 summary): dietary copper is absorbed in the gut and taken up by the liver; in hepatocytes the copper-transporting ATPase ATP7B (1) excretes copper into bile and (2) incorporates copper into ceruloplasmin, a serum ferroxidase responsible for ~90% of copper transport from the liver. Wilson card: autosomal recessive; two pathogenic ATP7B variants (chromosome 13) → impaired biliary excretion → hepatic copper retention → overflow to brain, cornea and other organs; apoceruloplasmin (without copper) has a shorter half-life.

cues.text: Copper from food is absorbed in the gut and taken up by the liver.
In liver cells, the copper pump ATP7B does two jobs: it excretes copper into bile, and it loads copper onto ceruloplasmin, which carries about 90 percent of the copper leaving the liver.
Wilson disease is autosomal recessive: two faulty copies of ATP7B on chromosome 13. Biliary excretion fails, and copper builds up in the liver.
Copper then spills over into the brain, the cornea and other organs. Ceruloplasmin without copper is cleared faster, so levels are often low, but not always.

scenes.title: No single test is the gold standard
scenes.altText: Test cards (AASLD 2023 summary; Schroeder 2021). Ceruloplasmin: typically low in Wilson disease (often < 14 mg/dL; normal > 20; enzymatic oxidase assay preferred over immunologic methods) but poor predictive value — many low values are not Wilson disease (e.g., cirrhosis, impaired liver function lowers it) and a normal value does not exclude it. Basal 24-h urinary copper: reflects non-ceruloplasmin-bound copper; > 100 µg/24 h in symptomatic patients (> 40 µg may indicate Wilson disease in asymptomatic individuals). Hepatic copper: > 250 µg/g dry weight. Kayser-Fleischer rings (slit lamp or OCT): present in ~90% with neurological disease, absent in ~60% with hepatic disease; not pathognomonic (cholestatic disease). ATP7B genetic testing; the Leipzig score combines clinical and biochemical findings.

cues.text: There is no single gold-standard test. Ceruloplasmin is usually low, often below 14, but its predictive value is poor: other liver diseases and cirrhosis lower it, and a normal value does not exclude Wilson disease.
A basal 24-hour urine copper reflects the free, non-ceruloplasmin copper. Above 100 micrograms per day is typical in symptomatic patients.
Liver tissue copper above 250 micrograms per gram dry weight supports the diagnosis.
Kayser-Fleischer rings, copper in the cornea seen by slit lamp, are present in about 90 percent of patients with neurological disease, but absent in about 60 percent with liver disease.
ATP7B gene testing helps, and the Leipzig score combines clinical and laboratory findings into one diagnosis.

scenes.title: Putting it together
scenes.altText: Work-up card (AASLD 2023): liver biochemistries, CBC and INR, serum ceruloplasmin, basal 24-h urinary copper, slit-lamp/OCT for KF rings, neurological evaluation, ATP7B molecular testing — a combination of assessments. Treatment card: initial therapy for symptomatic patients includes a chelating agent (D-penicillamine or trientine, which promote urinary copper excretion; trientine may be better tolerated); zinc is generally well tolerated and similar in efficacy to penicillamine, though hepatic treatment failure was more frequent with zinc in one analysis. Monitoring includes serum copper and ceruloplasmin trends and urinalysis on chelators. Back to the hook: a normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude Wilson disease → order 24-h urinary copper, slit-lamp exam and ATP7B testing.

cues.text: The guidance recommends a combination: liver tests, blood count and INR, ceruloplasmin, a basal 24-hour urine copper, a slit-lamp or OCT eye examination, neurological assessment, and ATP7B gene testing.
Symptomatic patients start with a chelator, D-penicillamine or trientine, which pull copper out in the urine. Trientine may be better tolerated.
Zinc is well tolerated and broadly as effective as penicillamine, although liver treatment failure was more common with zinc in one study.
During treatment, labs follow serum copper and ceruloplasmin trends, and urinalysis on chelators.
Back to our patient: the normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude Wilson disease. Order a 24-hour urine copper, a slit-lamp exam and ATP7B testing.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Normal ceruloplasmin rules out Wilson disease” (✓ normal values do not exclude it; use urine copper, KF rings, genetics); “Low ceruloplasmin proves Wilson disease” (✓ many low values are other liver disease or cirrhosis); “No KF rings = no Wilson disease” (✓ absent in ~60% of hepatic presentations).

cues.text: Trap one: a normal ceruloplasmin rules out Wilson disease. No: normal values do not exclude it. Use urine copper, eye examination and genetics.
Trap two: a low ceruloplasmin proves Wilson disease. No: many patients with low values have other liver disease or cirrhosis.
Trap three: no Kayser-Fleischer rings means no Wilson disease. They are absent in about 60 percent of patients who present with liver disease.

scenes.title: Copper can’t get out
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Wilson’s copper can’t get OUT (ATP7B → bile), so it piles up IN — the liver, then the brain and the eye.” Tokens: Urine copper ↑ · Liver copper ↑ · Ceruloplasmin: usually ↓, never decisive. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: Wilson copper cannot get out. ATP7B cannot push it into bile, so it piles up in the liver, then the brain and the eye. Urine and liver copper go up; ceruloplasmin is usually down but never decisive alone.
Where it breaks: other liver diseases can show borderline results; urine copper can rise in other liver injury; and no single cut-off settles the diagnosis, which is why scores combine findings.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Wilson: AR ATP7B → copper can’t enter bile → liver, brain, cornea · no single gold-standard test”, “Ceruloplasmin usually low but normal doesn’t exclude · 24-h urine Cu > 100 µg · liver Cu > 250 µg/g · KF rings ~90% neuro · chelators or zinc”.

cues.text: Wilson disease is diagnosed by combining tests, because ceruloplasmin can be normal: a raised 24-hour urine copper, liver copper above 250 µg/g, Kayser-Fleischer rings and ATP7B testing carry the decision.

props.label: AR ATP7B → copper can’t enter bile · no single gold-standard test
Cp normal ≠ excluded · urine Cu > 100 µg/24 h · liver > 250 µg/g · KF · ATP7B

explanation.what: Plain language: in Wilson disease the liver cannot get rid of copper into bile, so copper builds up in the liver and then the brain and eyes; because no single blood test is decisive, several tests are combined. Scientific terms: ATP7B, autosomal recessive, ceruloplasmin (ferroxidase), apoceruloplasmin, non-ceruloplasmin-bound copper, basal 24-hour urinary copper, hepatic copper (µg/g dry weight), Kayser-Fleischer rings, Leipzig score, chelation (D-penicillamine, trientine), zinc.
explanation.why: ATP7B both excretes hepatic copper into bile and incorporates copper into ceruloplasmin. Loss of function causes hepatic copper retention and overflow; apoceruloplasmin has a shorter half-life, so ceruloplasmin is often low — but other liver disease also lowers it and some patients have normal values.
explanation.measure: Ceruloplasmin typically < 14 mg/dL in WD (normal > 20), poor predictive value; basal 24-h urinary copper > 100 µg (> 1.6 µmol) in symptomatic patients, > 40 µg may indicate WD in asymptomatic individuals; hepatic copper > 250 µg/g dry weight; KF rings ~90% neurological, absent ~60% hepatic (Alkhouri 2023). Enzymatic oxidase ceruloplasmin assay preferred; cirrhosis lowers ceruloplasmin; KF rings not pathognomonic (Schroeder 2021).
explanation.differs: Wilson disease (low/normal ceruloplasmin, high urine and liver copper) vs other chronic liver disease (ceruloplasmin can be low from impaired synthesis; hepatic copper can be raised in cholestasis).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: whether normal ceruloplasmin excludes WD, urine copper and hepatic copper cut-offs, KF rings, ATP7B and AR inheritance, chelation therapy.

mnemonic.text: Wilson’s copper can’t get OUT, so it piles up IN — liver, then brain and eye.
mnemonic.explanation: ATP7B failure blocks biliary excretion: urine and liver copper rise, KF rings appear, ceruloplasmin is usually (not always) low.
mnemonic.limitation: Other liver diseases give borderline results; urine copper can rise in other liver injury; no single cut-off decides — scores combine findings.

analogyLimitations: “Can’t get out” simplifies a two-function transporter (bile excretion and ceruloplasmin loading).
Treatment details are outlined, not dosing guidance.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old with tremor and raised transaminases has a ceruloplasmin of 23 mg/dL (reference > 20). What is the best next step?

options.text: Basal 24-hour urinary copper, slit-lamp examination and ATP7B testing
options.rationale: Correct. A normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude Wilson disease; combine other tests.
Incorrect. Normal ceruloplasmin values do not exclude the diagnosis.
Incorrect. Ceruloplasmin alone has poor predictive value.
Incorrect. The diagnosis should be established first by a combination of assessments.

questions.stem: Which result most strongly supports Wilson disease in a symptomatic patient?

options.rationale: Correct. > 100 µg/24 h is typical of symptomatic Wilson disease and reflects free copper.

options.text: Ceruloplasmin of 18 mg/dL in a patient with cirrhosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cirrhosis itself can lower ceruloplasmin; this value is not specific.

options.text: Hepatic copper of 60 µg/g dry weight
options.rationale: Incorrect. The supportive threshold is > 250 µg/g.
Incorrect. Absence does not support or exclude WD; rings are absent in ~60% of hepatic cases.

questions.stem: What is the molecular defect in Wilson disease?

options.text: Biallelic ATP7B variants impairing biliary copper excretion
options.rationale: Correct. Autosomal recessive ATP7B defects (chromosome 13) cause hepatic copper retention.

options.text: A dominant mutation in the ceruloplasmin gene
options.rationale: Incorrect. Low ceruloplasmin is a consequence, not the primary defect.

options.text: A defect in intestinal copper absorption
options.rationale: Incorrect. The defect is hepatic excretion of copper into bile, not absorption.

options.text: Excess dietary copper absorption with normal excretion
options.rationale: Incorrect. The defect is excretion into bile.
